power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "P ≥0.05", Text = "None of these risk differences differed significantly from that in the eGFR ≥60 group (all P ≥0.05) (Table 3; Figure 2)."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.title: Non-Significant P Value Check
stat_p_nonsig.summary_text: We found 1 non-significant p value that should be checked for appropriate interpretation.

table.formatted: None of these risk differences differed significantly from that in the eGFR ≥60 group (all P ≥0.05) (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">3</ref>; Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>).
table.expanded: None of these risk differences differed significantly from that in the eGFR ≥60 group (all P ≥0.05) (Table 3; Figure 2).

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "P ≥0.05", Sentence = "None of these risk differences differed significantly from that in the eGFR ≥60 group (all P ≥0.05) (Table 3; Figure 2)."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

text.text: Background: Socioeconomic position is associated with kidney disease, but it remains unclear whether these differences are greater for worsening kidney function than for a first recorded diagnosis.
We examined how household income, education, and neighborhood deprivation relate to mortality and kidney outcomes.
We conducted a retrospective cohort study involving 218,098 individuals using data from the All of Us Research Program, with follow-up to January 1, 2025.
Primary outcomes involved all-cause mortality and sustained 40% estimated glomerular filtration rate decline.
Secondary outcomes were incident recorded chronic kidney disease (CKD) diagnosis, incident recorded CKD category G3a or worse, and kidney failure.
We also evaluated income inequalities and estimated standardized 3-year mortality risks for each baseline kidney state.
Median follow-up was 3.62 years for mortality and 2.76 years for kidney outcomes.

Among 218,098 individuals, 4,777 deaths, 6,423 sustained declines, 7,870 incident recorded chronic kidney disease diagnoses, 4,716 incident category G3a-or-worse events, and 1,799 kidney failure events were observed.

Adjusted hazard ratios (95% CIs) for household income below $25,000 compared with $200,000 or more were 2.68 (2.31-3.12), 3.57 (3.08-4.13), 2.13 (1.90-2.38), 2.15 (1.86-2.49), and 3.08 (2.30-4.11), respectively.
Relative index of inequality estimates were approximately twice as large for sustained decline and kidney failure than for recorded CKD diagnosis.
Within baseline kidney states, standardized 3-year absolute mortality differences by income did not differ significantly across states.
The main limitations are the observational design, baseline creatinine measured up to a year after the survey, and outcome ascertainment from health records that may differ by income.
Conclusions: Lower income was associated with higher mortality and greater risk of all kidney outcomes.
Education and neighborhood deprivation showed different patterns of association, which supports considering individual and neighborhood circumstances together.

Health inequities are systematic, avoidable, and unfair differences in health outcomes and access to healthcare between social groups, rooted in unequal social, economic, and environmental conditions (1).
text.formatted: Health inequities are systematic, avoidable, and unfair differences in health outcomes and access to healthcare between social groups, rooted in unequal social, economic, and environmental conditions <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(1)</ref>.

text.text: Globally, an estimated 2.1 billion people, which represents 26% of the global population, experienced financial hardship from out-of-pocket healthcare spending in 2022.
Approximately 75% of people in the poorest groups faced financial hardship from healthcare costs compared with fewer than 4% in the richest groups (2).
These inequalities are particularly relevant to kidney health (3, 4).
text.formatted: These inequalities are particularly relevant to kidney health <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">4)</ref>.

text.text: Among 14,086 participants in the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities (ARIC) study with a median follow-up duration of 23 years, lower income was associated with a 15% steeper decline in estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) and a higher risk of kidney failure (adjusted HR, 1.50; 95% CI, 1.14-1.98) compared with high income (5).
text.formatted: Among 14,086 participants in the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities (ARIC) study with a median follow-up duration of 23 years, lower income was associated with a 15% steeper decline in estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) and a higher risk of kidney failure (adjusted HR, 1.50; 95% CI, 1.14-1.98) compared with high income <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(5)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, among 5.6 million Japanese working adults, the lowest income decile, compared with the highest, was associated with rapid kidney function decline (adjusted OR, 1.70; 95% CI, 1.67-1.73) and higher risk of renal replacement therapy initiation (adjusted HR, 1.65; 95% CI, 1.47-1.86) (6).
text.formatted: Similarly, among 5.6 million Japanese working adults, the lowest income decile, compared with the highest, was associated with rapid kidney function decline (adjusted OR, 1.70; 95% CI, 1.67-1.73) and higher risk of renal replacement therapy initiation (adjusted HR, 1.65; 95% CI, 1.47-1.86) <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(6)</ref>.

text.text: In the Scottish GLOMMS-CORE study, people with early kidney disease living in unemployed households had higher mortality than those in professional households (adjusted HR, 1.77; 95% CI, 1.60-1.96) (7).
text.formatted: In the Scottish GLOMMS-CORE study, people with early kidney disease living in unemployed households had higher mortality than those in professional households (adjusted HR, 1.77; 95% CI, 1.60-1.96) <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(7)</ref>.

text.text: Both household and neighborhood deprivation were associated with higher mortality, with the poorest outcomes among people experiencing both.
These findings highlight the role of socioeconomic inequalities within adverse renal outcomes and mortality.
Nevertheless, limited evidence exists about the association of income inequalities in recorded chronic kidney disease and sustained kidney function decline.

We therefore conducted a large-scale cohort study using the All of Us Research Program Controlled Tier Dataset examine the role of socioeconomic inequalities across adverse renal outcomes and mortality.

We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the All of Us Research Program Controlled Tier Dataset (version 9, C2025Q4R6) which enrolls adults across the United States with deliberate recruitment of underrepresented populations in biomedical research (8).
text.formatted: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the All of Us Research Program Controlled Tier Dataset (version 9, C2025Q4R6) which enrolls adults across the United States with deliberate recruitment of underrepresented populations in biomedical research <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(8)</ref>.

text.text: Participants provided informed consent, and the All of Us program protocol was approved by its Institutional Review Board (protocol 11-01139).
The Yale University Institutional Review Board determined that this analysis was not human subjects research (protocol 2000043320; July 14, 2026).
Counts of 1 to 20 were suppressed in accordance with All of Us policy.
This study followed the STROBE reporting guideline (9).
text.formatted: This study followed the STROBE reporting guideline <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(9)</ref>.

text.text: The study included participants aged 18 years or older with linked electronic health record data, determined baseline kidney state, positive mortality follow-up after the index date, and provided substantive responses to both household income and educational attainment.
The index date was the earliest response to either socioeconomic item and could precede the other response.
Participants without a creatinine measurement from which estimated glomerular filtration rate could be calculated were eligible only if kidney failure or kidney transplantation could be identified.
Missing responses, including "Skip" and "Prefer not to answer," were excluded.
Household income and educational attainment were obtained from participant surveys.
Educational attainment was categorized as less than high school, high school or equivalent, some college, or college graduate or above.
Income was not adjusted for household size.
Neighborhood deprivation was the program-supplied index based on 3-digit ZIP code and was categorized into tertiles using the otherwise-eligible source cohort.
Neighborhood deprivation values that were unavailable were coded separately as a different category.
Income, education, and neighborhood deprivation were included in the primary models.
Estimated glomerular filtration rate was calculated from serum creatinine using the race-free 2021 CKD-EPI equation (10).
text.formatted: Estimated glomerular filtration rate was calculated from serum creatinine using the race-free 2021 CKD-EPI equation <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(10)</ref>.

text.text: Baseline creatinine was the measurement closest to the index within 365 days before or after that date.
Creatinine values between 0.1 and 20 were retained and treated as mg/dL; recorded units were not used to filter or convert values.
Participants without kidney failure or transplantation were classified into GFR categories G1 (≥90), G2 (60-89), G3a (45-59), G3b (30-44), G4 (15-29), or G5 (<15 mL/min/1.73 m²).
text.formatted: Participants without kidney failure or transplantation were classified into GFR categories G1 (≥90), G2 (60-89), G3a (45-59), G3b (30-44), G4 (15-29), or G5 (<15 mL/min/1.73 m²).

text.text: Kidney failure and transplantation were classified as separate baseline states, with transplantation taking precedence.
Kidney failure was identified from diagnostic codes indicating chronic kidney failure or dialysis dependence or from dialysis records on at least 2 dates separated by at least 90 days.
Kidneyfailure qualification used the available longitudinal record, with onset assigned to the earliest dialysis/ESKD record; later evidence could retrospectively qualify a date before index.
Kidney transplantation was identified from status or procedure records.
Detailed information is provided in Supplementary Methods.
The primary outcomes were all-cause mortality and a sustained 40% decline in eGFR.
Decline required an eGFR ≤60% of baseline after the baseline measurement, confirmed by another qualifying value at least 30 days later.
The event was dated to the first qualifying measurement.
Qualifying low eGFR values did not need to be consecutive, and the confirmation period was not explicitly restricted by death or the administrative end of follow-up.
Prevalent recorded CKD was identified when the assigned first-record date was on or before the index date, although confirmation of CKD could occur after the index date.
Further details are provided in Supplementary Methods.
Secondary outcomes were a first recorded diagnosis of chronic kidney disease (CKD), first recorded CKD category G3a or worse, and kidney failure.
Recorded CKD outcomes required one inpatient diagnosis or qualifying diagnoses on at least two different dates, with the event dated to the first record.
The kidney-failure outcome was the first qualifying dialysis or ESKD record, as defined above, or kidney transplantation, whichever occurred first.
Participants with recorded CKD, kidney failure, or transplantation at baseline were excluded from the recorded-diagnosis analyses.
Participants with baseline kidney failure or transplantation were excluded from the decline and kidney-failure analyses.
The decline analysis also required a baseline eGFR estimate.
Each analysis required positive follow-up.
For kidney outcomes, follow-up ended at qualifying outcome, death, last qualifying clinical contact, or January 1, 2025, whichever occurred first.
Mortality follow-up ended at death or January 1, 2025, without censoring at the last EHR contact.
Deaths were identified from the program's death records, using the earliest recorded date for each participant.
Adjusted hazard ratios and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated using Cox models with the Efron method of handling ties.
Household income, education, and neighborhood deprivation were included in primary Cox models as categorical variables.
Models were adjusted for age, sex, race, and ethnicity.

Race and ethnicity were self-reported in the program's basics survey and were included as social categories to account for social patterning of socioeconomic position, kidney disease, and care; the categories are listed in the Supplementary Methods.
Age was modeled linearly.
Remaining variables were treated as categorical.
Reference groups were income ≥$200,000, college graduate or above, and the least deprived neighborhood tertile.
For nonfatal outcomes, cause-specific models censored participants at death.
The proportional hazards assumption was assessed with scaled Schoenfeld residual tests.
Follow-up was split at 2 years, and income associations were estimated separately within each period with the same covariate set.
When the assumption was not met, overall HRs were interpreted as summaries of the associations over follow-up.
Income inequalities were also summarized using the relative index of inequality (RII) and slope index of inequality (SII) (11).
text.formatted: Income inequalities were also summarized using the relative index of inequality (RII) and slope index of inequality (SII) <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(11)</ref>.

text.text: For each outcome cohort, income groups were ranked from highest to lowest.
Each group received a ridit score equal to the proportion of participants in higher-income groups plus half the proportion in that group.
RII compared the extremes of income rank using Cox models adjusted for sex, age, race, and ethnicity.

The RII is the hazard ratio for a one-unit change in ridit score, the modeled contrast between the lowest-and highest-income extremes of the distribution; values above 1 indicate higher hazard with lower income.
The indices summarize the total income gradient and were therefore not adjusted for education or neighborhood deprivation.
SII used population-weighted regression of the five crude income-category rates on ridit scores and was expressed per 1000 person-years.
Further details are provided in Supplementary Methods.

In exploratory analyses, we estimated the income trend per $10,000 within subgroups defined by race, sex, age, diabetes, and baseline kidney state, and the categorical socioeconomic associations with mortality within sex, race, and neighborhood-deprivation strata; a descriptive analysis repeated the income models among participants with prevalent recorded CKD at baseline.
SII confidence intervals were calculated using a t-distribution with three residual degrees of freedom.
Aalen-Johansen estimator was used for unadjusted 5-year kidney outcome cumulative incidence, with death treated as a competing event.

Associations between income and mortality within kidney function states were assessed using Cox models adjusted for the primary covariates, and an income-by-kidney-state interaction was tested using a likelihood-ratio test.

Standardized 3-year mortality risks were estimated separately for each kidney state using Kaplan-Meier-based infinitesimal-jackknife pseudo-observations and identity-link regression adjusted for the primary covariates.
HC1 robust standard errors were used to calculate Wald confidence intervals, without restricting their limits to the 0%-100% range.
Absolute risk differences were calculated by subtracting the estimated risk in the highest-income group from that in the lowest-income group.
Differences in risk differences across kidney states were assessed using eGFR ≥60 mL/min/1.73 m² as the reference, with variances summed from the separate, nonoverlapping state-specific models.
These cross-state comparisons were considered descriptive.
A pooled Cox model with income-by-state interaction provided standardized 2-and 3-year risks as a sensitivity analysis, with percentile intervals from 300 participant-level bootstrap replicates.
Other sensitivity analyses changed mortality censoring, kidney-failure chronicity requirements, or eligibility based on numeric baseline eGFR.
Among 481,849 individuals who met the age and follow-up criteria, 218,098 were included in the study.

Exclusions were 207,335 individuals whose baseline kidney state could not be determined, 54,482 without a household income response, and 1,934 without an education response (Supplementary Table S1; Supplementary Figure S9).

text.text: Mean age was 54.3 years, and 132,327 individuals (60.7%) were female.
Median follow-up was 2.76 years for kidney outcomes, and 3.62 years for mortality.
Compared with individuals in the highest income category, those in the lowest category were younger, had lower educational attainment, and more often lived in deprived neighborhoods (Table 1).

text.text: At baseline, 2,440 individuals had kidney failure, and 1,955 had received a kidney transplant.
During follow-up, 4,777 individuals died.
Among the 209,916 individuals included in the kidney-function decline analysis, 6,423 experienced a sustained 40% decline in eGFR.

Compared with participants with household income of $200,000 or more, those with income below $25,000 had higher hazards of mortality (adjusted HR, 2.68; 95% CI, 2.31-3.12) and sustained kidney function decline (adjusted HR, 3.57; 95% CI, 3.08-4.13).
Among 194,814 individuals included in the recorded CKD analyses, 7,870 had a first recorded CKD diagnosis and 4,716 had a first recorded diagnosis of CKD category G3a or worse.
Kidney failure occurred in 1,799 of 209,916 eligible individuals.

Comparing the lowest with the highest income category, adjusted HRs were 2.13 (95% CI, 1.90-2.38) for recorded CKD diagnosis, 2.15 (95% CI, 1.86-2.49) for recorded CKD category G3a or worse, and 3.08 (95% CI, 2.30-4.11) for kidney failure (Table 2; Figure 1).

text.text: Among individuals who had not completed high school, the adjusted HR for mortality was 1.41 (95% CI, 1.25-1.60) compared with college graduates.
The corresponding adjusted hazard ratio for sustained eGFR decline was 1.42 (95% CI, 1.29-1.58).
Both models were adjusted for household income, neighborhood deprivation, and demographic covariates.
Individuals living in the most deprived neighborhood tertile had higher hazards of all four kidney outcomes than those in the least deprived tertile.
Among the four kidney outcomes, the HR was lowest for sustained eGFR decline at 1.09 (95% CI, 1.02-1.17) and highest for kidney failure at 1.42 (95% CI, 1.25-1.61).
No association with mortality was observed for this comparison (HR, 1.00; 95% CI, 0.93-1.08) (Supplementary Table S5; Supplementary Figure S1).

text.text: Inequality was greater for sustained eGFR decline and kidney failure than for outcomes based on recorded CKD diagnoses.
The relative index of inequality was 6.84 (95% CI, 6.15-7.61) for sustained eGFR decline and 6.06 (95% CI, 4.94-7.44) for kidney failure.
Lower estimates were observed for recorded CKD diagnosis (3.02; 95% CI, 2.76-3.30) and CKD category G3a or worse (2.94; 95% CI, 2.62-3.31).
For mortality, the relative index of inequality was 4.70 (95% CI, 4.17-5.29).
Sustained eGFR decline also showed the largest crude absolute inequality, with a slope index of 16.98 additional events per 1,000 person-years (95% CI, 10.27-23.70).
Differences in inequality estimates across outcomes were described but not formally tested (Supplementary Table S5; Supplementary Figure S10).

text.text: Among individuals with baseline eGFR ≥60 mL/min/1.73 m², those in the lowest income category had a higher risk of mortality than those in the highest category (adjusted HR, 2.73; 95% CI, 2.28-3.26).

The corresponding HR was 1.86 (95% CI, 1.32-2.61) for eGFR 30-59 mL/min/1.73 m², 1.24 (95% CI, 0.50-3.05) for eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m², 1.31 (95% CI, 0.58-2.94) for kidney failure, and 1.71 (95% CI, 0.70-4.16) for kidney transplantation.

The overall interaction between income and baseline kidney state was nominally significant (likelihood ratio χ² = 26.5; 16 degrees of freedom; P = 0.047), although the state-specific estimates were imprecise (Table 3).

text.text: Among individuals with eGFR ≥60 mL/min/1.73 m², standardized 3-year mortality risks were 1.77% in the lowest income category and 0.73% in the highest, a difference of 1.04 percentage points (95% CI, 0.81-1.27).
Among those with eGFR 30-59, risks were 5.09% and 3.21%, respectively, a difference of 1.88 percentage points (95% CI, 0.44-3.33).

Risk differences were 7.51 percentage points (95% CI, 0.16-14.85) for eGFR <30, 2.10 percentage points (95% CI, -5.50 to 9.70) for kidney failure, and 2.20 percentage points (95% CI, -2.33 to 6.73) for kidney transplantation.

text.text: None of these risk differences differed significantly from that in the eGFR ≥60 group (all P ≥0.05) (Table 3; Figure 2).

text.text: The proportional hazards assumption was not met for mortality, sustained eGFR decline, or either recorded CKD outcome.
However, the association between lower income and higher hazards remained during both the first 2 years and subsequent follow-up.
For mortality, the HR comparing the lowest with the highest income category was 2.18 (95% CI, 1.74-2.73) during the first two years and 3.12 (95% CI, 2.55-3.81) thereafter.
The corresponding HRs for sustained eGFR decline were 4.21 (95% CI, 3.42-5.18) and 2.95 (95% CI, 2.40-3.64), respectively (Supplementary Table S8).

text.text: With death treated as a competing event, the unadjusted 5-year cumulative incidence of all kidney outcomes was higher in the lowest income category than in the highest.

The 5-year cumulative incidence in the lowest and highest income categories was 8.00% and 1.95%, respectively, for sustained eGFR decline; 7.49% and 3.84% for recorded CKD diagnosis; 4.33% versus 2.23% for recorded CKD category G3a or worse; and 2.32% versus 0.46% for kidney failure (Supplementary Table S7; Supplementary Figure S2).

text.text: In sensitivity analyses, censoring mortality follow-up at the last recorded EHR contact yielded an HR of 2.95 (95% CI, 2.38-3.65), whereas the primary analysis included 2,256 deaths occurring after the last EHR contact.
Restricting the analysis to individuals with a numeric baseline eGFR yielded a mortality HR of 2.70 (95% CI, 2.32-3.14).
When the chronicity requirements for kidney failure were removed, the number of events increased to 2,564, with an HR of 2.78 (95% CI, 2.21-3.51) (Supplementary Table S10; Supplementary Figure S4).

text.text: Our analysis of this large-scale observational All of Us cohort revealed that lower income was associated with higher mortality and all four kidney outcomes.

In particular, income-gradient estimates were numerically larger for sustained kidney function decline and kidney failure than for a first recorded CKD diagnosis, with substantial differences also evident in the 5-year cumulative incidence of kidney outcomes.
Education and neighborhood deprivation demonstrated different patterns of association, highlighting the importance of considering individual and neighborhood socioeconomic circumstances together.
Interestingly, incomerelated mortality hazard ratios were numerically lower in more advanced baseline kidney states.
Income associations also varied over follow-up, with mortality hazard ratios numerically larger later and hazard ratios for sustained kidney function decline larger earlier.
Previous large-scale cohort studies have already linked socioeconomic disadvantage to kidney function decline, mortality, and kidney failure.

In a nationwide Korean cohort of 7,405,715 adults with a median follow-up duration of 4.8 years, individuals in the lowest income decile had a higher risk of incident CKD than those in the sixth decile (adjusted HR, 1.30; 95% CI, 1.26-1.33) (12).
text.formatted: In a nationwide Korean cohort of 7,405,715 adults with a median follow-up duration of 4.8 years, individuals in the lowest income decile had a higher risk of incident CKD than those in the sixth decile (adjusted HR, 1.30; 95% CI, 1.26-1.33) <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(12)</ref>.

text.text: The association was similar when incident CKD required both a ≥25% decline in eGFR and an eGFR below 60 mL/min/1.73 m² (adjusted HR, 1.32; 95% CI, 1.27-1.37).

Similarly, among 1,405,016 English primary-care patients followed for a median of 7.5 years, those living in the most deprived 20% of areas had higher hazards of CKD stages 4-5 and ESRD than those in the least deprived 20% (age-and sex-adjusted HRs, 1.76; 95% CI, 1.68-1.84 and 1.82; 95% CI, 1.56-2.12, respectively) (13).

Furthermore, among 2,761 individuals with prevalent CKD stage 3 or 4, annual household income below $20,000 was associated with higher all-cause mortality than income of $20,000 or more (adjusted HR, 1.58; 95% CI, 1.24-2.00) (14).
text.formatted: Furthermore, among 2,761 individuals with prevalent CKD stage 3 or 4, annual household income below $20,000 was associated with higher all-cause mortality than income of $20,000 or more (adjusted HR, 1.58; 95% CI, 1.24-2.00) <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(14)</ref>.

text.text: Our study further extends prior findings in a large, ethnically diverse U.S. cohort with linked longitudinal electronic health records by jointly examining income, education, and neighborhood deprivation in relation to sustained kidney function decline, recorded CKD, kidney failure, and mortality, while quantifying 5-year kidney-event incidence across income groups and evaluating mortality inequalities across baseline kidney states.
Importantly, the income gradients were accompanied by substantial differences in 5-year kidney outcomes.
At 5 years, estimated cumulative incidence of sustained kidney function decline was 8.00% in the lowest-income group, compared with 1.95% in the highest-income group.
The corresponding estimates for kidney failure were 2.32% and 0.46%.
These findings are consistent with previous U.S. studies showing greater burden of kidney failure among individuals with lower incomes and in counties with greater poverty.

Among 79,943 individuals in the Southern Community Cohort Study, annual household income below $15,000 was associated with a higher risk of kidney failure than income of $15,000 or more (adjusted HR, 1.5; 95% CI, 1.2-1.8) (15).
text.formatted: Among 79,943 individuals in the Southern Community Cohort Study, annual household income below $15,000 was associated with a higher risk of kidney failure than income of $15,000 or more (adjusted HR, 1.5; 95% CI, 1.2-1.8) <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(15)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, a national U.S. analysis also found that the excess incidence of kidney failure in highpoverty compared with low-poverty counties increased from 42.8 cases per million in 2000-2005 to 100.1 cases per million in 2012-2017, despite an overall national decline in kidney failure incidence (16).
text.formatted: Similarly, a national U.S. analysis also found that the excess incidence of kidney failure in highpoverty compared with low-poverty counties increased from 42.8 cases per million in 2000-2005 to 100.1 cases per million in 2012-2017, despite an overall national decline in kidney failure incidence <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(16)</ref>.

text.text: Our study extends these reports on kidney failure by also quantifying income inequalities in sustained kidney function decline confirmed by repeated measurements.

Incorporating all income categories demonstrated that sustained kidney function decline had numerically the largest relative and absolute income inequalities (RII, 6.84; SII, 16.98 events per 1,000 person-years).
Furthermore, education and neighborhood deprivation demonstrated different patterns of associations across outcomes.
Lower education was associated with higher risks of mortality and sustained kidney function decline.
On the other hand, greater neighborhood deprivation was associated with adverse kidney outcomes despite demonstrating no clear associations with mortality.
These findings highlight the importance of considering both individual and neighborhood socioeconomic circumstances when examining inequalities across kidney outcomes.

Among 5,095 individuals in the German CKD cohort with a follow-up duration of 6.5 years, lower education was associated with higher mortality (age-and sex-adjusted HR, 1.48; 95% CI, 1.16-1.90) and kidney failure requiring dialysis (HR, 1.54; 95% CI, 1.15-2.05) compared with higher education (17).
Nevertheless, these associations were no longer statistically significant after further adjustment for kidney disease severity and potential mediators, including income.

In the Cardiovascular Health Study of 4,735 individuals aged 65 years or older, those living in neighborhoods with the lowest socioeconomic status had a 50% higher risk of progressive CKD compared to those in the highest socioeconomic quartile, even after adjustment for demographic characteristics, baseline creatinine, and individual-level socioeconomic factors (18).

This association persisted after further adjustment for lifestyle factors, diabetes, and hypertension, whereas individual income and education were not independently associated with progressive CKD after accounting for the other SES measures.
In our broader large-scale U.S. adult cohort, lower education remained associated with mortality and sustained kidney function decline after accounting for income and neighborhood deprivation.
These findings suggest that income alone may not fully capture socioeconomic inequalities across kidney outcomes.
Moreover, relative income associations with mortality were numerically smaller among individuals with more advanced kidney disease.

Specifically, the adjusted mortality hazard ratio comparing the lowest-with the highest-income group was 2.73 (95% CI, 2.28-3.26) among participants with baseline eGFR ≥60 mL/min/1.73 m², compared with 1.24 (95% CI, 0.50-3.05) among those with eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m².
text.formatted: Specifically, the adjusted mortality hazard ratio comparing the lowest-with the highest-income group was 2.73 (95% CI, 2.28-3.26) among participants with baseline eGFR ≥60 mL/min/1.73 m², compared with 1.24 (95% CI, 0.50-3.05) among those with eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m².

text.text: Nevertheless, evidence of heterogeneity across kidney-function strata was weak, and estimates among participants with advanced kidney dysfunction were imprecise.

Furthermore, the standardized 3-year analysis did not establish differences in absolute mortality gaps across states, although the intervals were wide and the pooled Cox sensitivity analysis, which depends on a rejected proportionality assumption, suggested larger gaps in two states.
A similar numerical pattern was reported in a Grampian population study.

The adjusted mortality hazard ratio comparing residents of the most deprived areas with those in all other areas was 1.21 (95% CI, 1.14-1.28) among people presenting with eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m² and 1.11 (95% CI, 1.04-1.19) among those presenting with eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m² (3).
text.formatted: The adjusted mortality hazard ratio comparing residents of the most deprived areas with those in all other areas was 1.21 (95% CI, 1.14-1.28) among people presenting with eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m² and 1.11 (95% CI, 1.04-1.19) among those presenting with eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m² (3).

text.text: Our study complements this evidence by estimating standardized absolute differences in three-year mortality between income groups across baseline kidney states.
Income associations also varied over follow-up.
Comparing the lowest-with the highest-income group, the adjusted hazard ratio for mortality was 2.18 during the first two years of follow-up and 3.12 thereafter.
The corresponding hazard ratios for sustained kidney function decline were 4.21 and 2.95.
Although the strengths of these associations varied over time, income-related inequalities remained evident in both early and later follow-up.
These findings suggest that a single overall hazard ratio may obscure changes in the magnitude of income associations during follow-up.
Differences in participants' health at baseline or their use of healthcare potentially could explain these patterns; nevertheless, we did not test those explanations.
Future studies could potentially clarify why the associations varied over time.
Although our large-scale observational cohort study provides valuable insights into socioeconomic inequalities across kidney outcomes and mortality, several limitations should be acknowledged.
First, given the observational nature of the study, the observed associations should not be interpreted as causal relationships.

Second, socioeconomic circumstances were assessed only at baseline, so subsequent income changes were not captured, while neighborhood deprivation measured using three-digit ZIP codes may obscure local differences.
Third, incomplete EHR coverage and differences in testing and coding may have affected outcome detection.

Incident CKD was identified from diagnosis records and a laboratory definition based on repeated low eGFR values was not applied; recorded creatinine units were not verified; and deaths near the end of the data period may be incompletely captured because of reporting lag.
Some creatinine measurements used to assess baseline kidney function were obtained after the socioeconomic survey, creating uncertainty about kidney status at the time of income assessment.

Fourth, only 218,098 of 481,849 otherwise eligible participants had a determined kidney state and complete socioeconomic responses, so selection related to income, illness, and healthcare use is possible.
Finally, as the All of Us Research Program is a volunteer-based cohort, participants may differ from the general population, potentially limiting the generalizability of our findings.

Therefore, further studies with repeated socioeconomic assessments, more detailed neighborhood information, and standardized kidney function measurements are needed to clarify these associations and identify potential ways to reduce socioeconomic inequalities in kidney health.
